source.section: Fermat's Little Theorem and Euler's Totient Function

problem.text: Find the largest positive integer $n$ such that $n\phi(n)$ is a perfect square. ($\phi(n)$ is the number of integers $k$, $1 \le k \le n$ that are relatively prime to $n$)

steps.title: Where to start: write $n\phi(n)$ in prime powers
steps.body: A number is a perfect square exactly when every prime in its factorization has an even exponent. So we want the prime factorization of $n\phi(n)$. The totient formula is built from the primes of $n$: if $n = p_1^{e_1} p_2^{e_2} \cdots p_x^{e_x}$ with different primes $p_i$, then $$\phi(n) = p_1^{e_1 - 1}(p_1 - 1) \cdot p_2^{e_2 - 1}(p_2 - 1) \cdots p_x^{e_x - 1}(p_x - 1).$$

your_turn.prompt: Multiply by $n$. What is $n\phi(n)$ in terms of the $p_i$ and $e_i$?
your_turn.answer: $n\phi(n) = p_1^{2e_1 - 1}(p_1 - 1) \cdots p_x^{2e_x - 1}(p_x - 1)$, since each $p_i^{e_i} \cdot p_i^{e_i - 1} = p_i^{2e_i - 1}$.

steps.title: Look at the largest prime
steps.body: Suppose $n > 1$, so $n$ has at least one prime factor, and let $p$ be the largest one, with exponent $e$. The power $p^{2e-1}$ has an odd exponent. The only way the total exponent of $p$ could become even is if some factor $p_i - 1$ also contained $p$.

your_turn.prompt: Can $p$ divide any of the numbers $p_1 - 1, \dots, p_x - 1$?
your_turn.answer: No. Each $p_i - 1$ is positive and smaller than $p_i$, which is at most $p$, so all of its prime factors are less than $p$.

steps.title: The exponent of $p$ is odd
steps.body: So the exponent of $p$ in $n\phi(n)$ is exactly $2e - 1$, and $2e - 1$ is odd for every $e$. Think about what that says for the perfect-square condition.

your_turn.prompt: Check this on $n = 12$: find $\phi(12)$, factor $12\phi(12)$, and look at the exponent of $3$.
your_turn.answer: $\phi(12) = 4$ (the numbers $1, 5, 7, 11$), so $12\phi(12) = 48 = 2^4 \cdot 3$. The largest prime, $3$, has exponent $1$, which is odd, so $48$ is not a square.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: Every $n > 1$ has a prime factor, and its largest prime appears in $n\phi(n)$ with an odd exponent, so $n\phi(n)$ is not a perfect square. So no $n > 1$ works. That leaves $n = 1$: the only $k$ with $1 \le k \le 1$ is $k = 1$, and $\gcd(1, 1) = 1$, so $\phi(1) = 1$ and $1 \cdot \phi(1) = 1 = 1^2$. The only (and so the largest) such $n$ is **$1$**.
